panels.text: It sounds like the kind of question a kid asks at 2 AM. The kind adults smile at and say, "That's very interesting, dear."

panels.text: But in 1928, one of the most famous mathematicians alive asked this question seriously. And he expected the answer to be yes.

Abstract dramatic explosion of shattering golden mathematical symbols and equations breaking apart like glass against deep crimson and dark background, shards of formulas flying outward from center, bold dramatic white text in the center reads: "He was wrong." dramatic chiaroscuro lighting, bold and cinematic, editorial illustration style with ink lines

panels.text:
Spectacularly, beautifully, world-changingly wrong.

The story of how we found that out is the story of how computing was born. Not in a lab. Not in a factory. In the mind of a mathematician who liked to run long distances and think about impossible things.

panels.prompt: Silhouette of a young man running alone along a misty riverbank at golden-hour dusk, Cambridge gothic college spires in the distant background, scattered autumn leaves on the ground, reflections of the runner in still water, moody atmospheric perspective with layers of mist, dreamy contemplative mood, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes in earth tones with subtle red accent in the sky

panels.text: Who was the mathematician who asked the question? And who was the young man who proved him wrong?
